The menopausal transition, which is the period of time when a woman's ovaries produce fewer estrogen hormones and progesterone hormones, can have varying effects on a woman's quality of life. While some studies suggest that certain aspects of the menopausal transition may negatively impact quality of life, others find no significant effects.

A longitudinal study among Taiwanese women found that the decline in role limitations due to emotional problems was related to vasomotor symptoms, but not directly affected their overall quality of life. Another study on rural Chinese women concluded that delivery mode did not affect postpartum quality of life, suggesting that socio-cultural determinants may have a more significant impact.

However, research has shown that better ambulatory process of care is associated with improved health-related quality of life outcomes for patients with chronic disease. Additionally, patient-prosthesis mismatch after aortic valve replacement has been found to not affect survival or quality of life in elderly patients aged 75 years or older.

On the other hand, adjuvant aromatase inhibitors may increase cardiovascular risk in postmenopausal women with early breast cancer, according to some studies. The use of these medications was associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular events, particularly grade 3 and 4 congestive heart failure (CVAEs), compared to tamoxifen.

Finally, research on hospice care in nursing homes suggests that analgesic management of pain at the end of life can be improved by enrolling residents in hospice care. However, this does not appear to increase readmission rates or physician visits within 30 days after discharge from hospital.

Overall, while there is evidence suggesting that certain aspects of menopausal transition may negatively impact quality of life, other studies have found no significant effects. Further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between menopausal transition and overall quality of life.
